cues.text: Taken Captive at Sixteen
Born around 387 somewhere on the western coast of Roman Britain, Patrick was the son of a minor Roman official and church deacon.
In the remarkable spiritual autobiography he left behind, he tells us that he had cared little for the Christian faith of his upbringing.
At sixteen, Irish raiders swept down upon his family's estate and carried him off across the sea into slavery.
Sold to a chieftain in the north of Ireland, Patrick spent the following six years alone on a remote hillside tending sheep and pigs.
Exposed to hunger, cold, and isolation, it was here, in this very captivity he had every reason to resent, that he tells us his faith kindled at last.
So lukewarm before, it became a fire of constant, almost involuntary prayer—sometimes a hundred prayers offered in a single day and as many again through the night.
Escape and a Summons in a Dream
After six years, Patrick heard, in a dream, a voice telling him that a ship stood ready to carry him home.
He fled his captivity and walked some two hundred miles to a port he had never seen or been told of.
Against considerable odds, he secured passage on a ship that carried him, after further hardship, back at last to his family in Britain.
Any ordinary man might have counted such a deliverance the end of his story; for Patrick it proved instead only its true beginning.
Some years later, settled once more among his own people, he received another vision.
A man he called Victoricus bore letters from Ireland, whose voices, as he opened them, cried out as if with a single mouth: we beg you, holy youth, to come and walk once more among us .
A Reluctant, Determined Missionary
Patrick's own account makes clear that he felt poorly equipped for the mission he now believed God was asking of him.
His schooling had been interrupted by years of captivity, and he wrote all his life with an unpolished, apologetic awareness of his limited Latin learning.
That humility runs through every page of his surviving writing.
Yet nothing about this sense of inadequacy deterred him.
Ordained a bishop and sent, by tradition around the year 432, Patrick returned to the land of his enslavement.
He took up the mission earlier begun by a bishop named Palladius, this time not as a captive but as its apostle.
He was determined to bring the Gospel to a people Rome itself had never subdued and Christianity had barely touched.
Planting the Faith Across Ireland
Patrick's mission carried him across the length and breadth of an island still overwhelmingly pagan, confronting hostile chieftains and druidic resistance.
He founded churches and ordained clergy; his Confession also records the emergence of communities of Irish women who embraced a life of Christian dedication.
This practice would help give Irish monasticism its distinctively vigorous early character.
His own Confession was written late in life, partly in his own self-defense against unnamed accusers back in Britain who questioned his mission.

It records real dangers faced along the way—threats of death, attempted robbery, and constant physical hardship—met, in every instance, with the same unwavering trust in providence that had first taken root in him during his years as a captive shepherd.
A Letter Against Slave-Raiding
Among Patrick's surviving writings is a second document, his Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus , a fierce public denunciation of a British warlord's raiders.
They had slaughtered and enslaved a group of Patrick's own newly baptized Irish converts — a text remarkable for its passionate defense of his flock.
It also offers an unambiguous condemnation of the killing and enslavement of captives that had once claimed Patrick himself.
He never forgot, even decades later, exactly what it felt like to be dragged in chains from everything he had known.
Legacy
Patrick died, by long tradition, on 17 March, a date the whole world still marks as St. Patrick's Day.
He left behind a Christian Ireland that would, within a few generations, become one of the great centers of monastic learning and missionary energy in the whole of early medieval Europe.
His own plain, unadorned Confession was written in defense of a mission he was never entirely sure others believed in.
It remains one of the most moving personal testimonies to survive from the whole of Christian antiquity.
It bears witness to Patrick's conviction that God could transform the injustice he suffered into a calling through which he would serve the people of Ireland.
